new_statements.reading: Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress: an instrumental study of rhyme duration, F0 and intensity in 2-4-syllable words (in carrier sentences, several speakers) finds no culminative word-level prominence; the cues pattern with prosodic-word edges and final syllables. The catalog's weight-hedged coding rests on Goldstein & Nornang's (1978: xv) impressionistic textbook note ('the longer syllable tends to take primary stress'); Lim explicitly reviews and rejects the stress accounts (Meredith 1990, Monich 2011; Meredith's speaker is Kham-native) and argues the Proto-Tibetan σ2 stress survives only as the H tone of the second syllable. Contradicts the catalog: Tibetan (Lhasa) should be flagged as a contested / stressless-candidate record (tone-only), not weight-sensitive.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tibetan has an empty rule; the existing statement (Lim 2018, instrumental, Lhasa) says Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress. Jäschke (1883, impressionistic, describing the pronunciation of written Tibetan with WT/CT dialect notes) asserts a word accent on the root / latter member of compounds, i.e. a different type (accent present, morphologically placed) from the stressless reading. It is compatible with Lim's remark that prominence cues in Lhasa mark prosodic-word edges and with the Proto-Tibetan second-syllable prominence Lim and Caplow discuss (compound-final accent), but as a claim about synchronic word stress it disagrees with Lim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: 'In such cases' = the postponed monosyllabic particles (§9.2-3) that form one word with a preceding nominal or verbal root: the accent goes to the root, not to the particle; in compounds it generally goes to the second (latter) member. An accented open syllable has a comparatively long vowel in Western Tibetan (Ladak) but is short in Central Tibetan (Lhasa). No position-counting rule; prominence is morphological (root vs. enclitic particle, compound-final).

new_statements.quote: In the Lhasa system, only a monosyllable is distinctive for the four contrastive pitches. The non-initial syllable in polysyllabic words is not contrastive for pitch height (or voice quality) and is always overlaid with a high pitch, regardless of its pitch in isolation or citation form. A syllable which is falling in isolation is also falling when it is the final syllable of a polysyllabic word, otherwise it also loses its contrastiveness for level or falling melody. When a word ends in an unstressed syllable, the penultimate syllable carries the level/falling contrast.

Its Lhasa section (pp. 32-33, after Mazaudon 1977) is compatible with the existing Lim 2018 statement (tone-only, non-initial syllables high, no culminative stress) and adds the templatic word-tone characterization and the observation that final unstressed (particle) syllables shift the level/falling contrast to the penult. Nothing in it supports a positional word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhasa Tibetan is a word-tone (template) language: the four monosyllabic tones contrast only on the first syllable; non-initial syllables are non-contrastive and high; the level/falling contrast sits on the final syllable, or on the penult when the final syllable is an unstressed one (i.e. a particle). No word-stress placement rule is given for Lhasa; 'unstressed' is used of final grammatical syllables. This is Watters's summary of Mazaudon 1977, not his own Lhasa data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none for Lhasa. For Lhomi (own data, p. 40): 'When the first syllable is long it attracts stress, or perhaps it is because this syllable is stressed that it is lengthened'; for Dolpo (p. 35) a 'perceived stress on the second syllable' in high register is used as a transcription cue.
new_statements.exceptions: For Lhasa: word-final unstressed syllables shift the level/falling contrast to the penult. Own-data languages: Dolpo/Mugom tone templates (final syllable always high falling), Sherpa word tone, Lhomi/Dzongkha syllable tone.

tone_statements.quote: The tonal system can be characterized as a mixed level-contour tone system. It counts two levels: High and Low. ... Raising and falling tones are, in fact, allotones which appear with certain types of syllables, see 3.2. ... Therefore, there are two tonemes, High/Falling and Low/Rising. Each toneme has several surface representations (allotones) depending 1) on the type of the syllable; 2) the presence or absence of the glottal stop in the Auslaut; 3) the length of the tonal span (one or two syllables).

tone_statements.summary: Two level tonemes H, L; contours are allotones by syllable type/final glottal stop; culminative: one toneme per prosodic word (1st syll., span <=2); affixes toneless; downstep in phrases; no stress.

tone_statements.translation: Phonologically, the default tone value of Lhasa Tibetan is a high shape H: the high tone class is realized as H; the low tone class adds a low initial shape L in front, realized as LH. In addition, if there is a glottal-stop coda, a low tail L is added. ... We hold that the key is not the number of tones but the analysis of tone shapes and their differentiation ... Our acoustic study confirms that Lhasa Tibetan has a clear high vs low tonal distinction, but the tone shapes are closely tied to syllable structure, showing that its contour system is still developing.

readall_conflicts: Jäschke (1883, pp. 12-13) asserts a word accent that falls on the root rather than on postponed particles and, in compounds, generally on the latter member; this is an impressionistic 19th-century statement about the pronunciation of written Tibetan with Western/Central dialect notes. The existing statement (Lim 2018, instrumental, Lhasa) finds no word stress at all and treats Lhasa Tibetan as a stressless word-tone language. Watters (2002, pp. 32-33, summarizing Mazaudon 1977) describes Lhasa as a word-tone template system and speaks of word-final 'unstressed' syllables, which presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction between roots and particles but gives no word-stress position; this is compatible with both Jäschke's root-vs-particle accent and Lim's edge-marking cues. The real disagreement is therefore whether root-vs-particle prominence counts as word stress (Jäschke: yes; Lim: no, it is prosodic-word-edge marking plus H tone on the second syllable). The Tournadre & Dorje manual could not be opened, so its position is unknown.

sources.quote: In the Lhasa system, only a monosyllable is distinctive for the four contrastive pitches. The non-initial syllable in polysyllabic words is not contrastive for pitch height (or voice quality) and is always overlaid with a high pitch, regardless of its pitch in isolation or citation form. A syllable which is falling in isolation is also falling when it is the final syllable of a polysyllabic word, otherwise it also loses its contrastiveness for level or falling melody. When a word ends in an unstressed syllable, the penultimate syllable carries the level/falling contrast.

sources.note: The paper's own data are Dzongkha (Pasakha), Lhomi, Solu Sherpa, Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan, none of which is tibe1272, so its stress remarks on those languages are not about this language.
